name: Réunion
summary_text: Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France.  Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the metropolitan statute adopted in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate, which delivered President François Hollande's campaign pledge. Both houses had to approve the text.  Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, which made transphobic harassment a criminal matter; deputies Sergio Coronado and Elisabeth Pochon intervened in that debate. The provision is in force in Réunion.  Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. The government's three sub-amendments could limit the scope of that section.  Prison placement in France follows the sex recorded on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code. Transgender women held in male prisons therefore fall into a legal grey area and are, in the account of a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes'; the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. The placement rule is the framework that governs detainees in Réunion.  The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) found 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities in its opinion of 25 May 2021. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it carries recommendations addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion applies to the national framework covering Réunion.

name: Romania
summary_text: Romania decriminalised same-sex relations and the practice is legal nationwide. Outright International's country overview records that Government Ordinance 137/2000 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex and sexual orientation, while institutional follow-through on that protection is limited. There is no marriage and no civil-partnership regime: the 2018 referendum to amend the constitution failed on low turnout, and the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017. LGBTI organisations can register and operate.  Legal gender recognition exists and is court-based. In the Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi case, the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate reflecting the trans man's UK-recognised identity, and the Bucharest Tribunal rejected the appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates, making the decision definitive in March 2026. ACCEPT Romania announced the outcome on Trans Day of Visibility and urges others who have changed their documents in another European Union member state to pursue transcription in Romania.  The legal anchor is the Court of Justice of the European Union's ruling of October 2024, reported by Reuters, that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, which concerns recognition of a UK gender recognition certificate in Romania. The ruling builds on the position that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition.  A Council of Europe thematic review of January 2023, 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania', documents the national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering the legal and policy framework, applicable European Court of Human Rights case-law and international standards.  Official hostility intensified during 2025. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 records that anti-LGBTI rhetoric rose through the presidential campaign: candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February, Prime Minister Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes, and a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements. The National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint.  The ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report, whose Romania chapter was authored by ACCEPT, found that eight of nine country submissions reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people, and cites the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.  Public visibility carries visible risk. AP reported in June 2025 that tens of thousands marched on the twentieth anniversary of the Bucharest Pride march amid rising right-wing hostility toward LGBTQ+ Romanians.  The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024, covering 2023, records that the National Council for Combating Discrimination investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials.

sources.title: ILGA-Europe Annual Report - Romania ranking 2022 / 2026
sources.documents: EU-wide LGBTQ rights protection ranking; documents Romania ranked 26 of 27 EU countries in 2022 behind all except Poland, and degraded to lowest-ranked EU country in 2026 report.
sources.detail: Cited in text as 'advocacy group ILGA-Europe ranked Romania 26 out of 27' in 2022 and 'lowest ranked among all European Union countries' in 2026 report. No URL visible in text.

sources.title: Emergency Ordinance no. 89/2001 repealing Penal Code Art. 200
sources.documents: Decriminalization of homosexuality; eliminates Art. 200 (1-5 years imprisonment for same-sex relations, 2-7 years with coercion/minor, etc.) and adjusts sex offences to avoid discrimination. Came into force January 2002 after President Ion Iliescu signed.
sources.detail: Cited as 'Adrian Nastase's government adopted the Emergency Ordinance no. 89/2001, which eliminated Art. 200' - in force January 2002. Prior history: 1937 Code Art.431, 1948 extension, 1957 removal of 'public scandal', 1968 Art.200, 1996 amendment to public only. No URL visible.

sources.title: Romania Constitutional Court Decision December 2020 on gender identity education ban
sources.documents: Strikes down June 2020 parliament amendment to education law placing blanket ban on gender identity studies passed without public debate; key transgender-expression / free expression protection.
sources.detail: Text states 'In June 2020, it placed a blanket ban on the study of gender identity in education. The ban was struck down in December 2020 by Romania's Constitutional Court.' Plus University of Bucharest condemnation quote. No URL visible.

sources.title: Constitution Art. 48 and Civil Code Art. 259 - marriage definition
sources.documents: Legal bar to same-sex marriage/family protection; Constitution defines family as 'freely consented marriage between spouses' but Civil Code Art.259(1) restricts to 'union between a man and a woman'; same-sex couple cannot receive state protection as family.
sources.detail: Quoted verbatim: 'Article 48 - Family (1) The family shall be founded on a freely consented marriage between spouses...' and 'Article 259 - Marriage (1) Marriage shall be a freely consented union between a man and a woman'. No URL visible.

sources.title: European Court of Justice - Coman and Others, June 2018
sources.documents: Residence rights for same-sex spouses; rules same-sex spouses have same right of residence if marriage legally performed in EU country, following Romanian Constitutional Court referral of Romanian-American couple married in Belgium.
sources.detail: Cited as 'European Court of Justice ruled in June 2018 in Coman and Others that same-sex spouses have the same right of residence'. No URL visible.
